meta.title: Who really said "Virtue is harmony"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Pythagoras's own words: a tenet from the “Pythagorean memoirs” reported by Diogenes Laertius (Lives 8.33), in R. D. Hicks's 1925 translation.
meta.ogDescription: Pythagoras wrote nothing. The line is a Pythagorean school tenet that Diogenes Laertius reported second-hand (Lives 8.33), from memoirs later scholars call a forgery.

answer.label: Not Pythagoras’s own words — a later Pythagorean tenet
answer.authorDates: c. 570 – c. 490 BC · Greek philosopher of Samos and Croton
answer.sourceLine: Pythagoras wrote nothing. The line comes from Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 8.33, in a list of tenets that “Alexander in his Successions of Philosophers says that he found in the Pythagorean memoirs.” The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy ↗ calls those memoirs “a forgery dating sometime around 200 BCE.” The exact English wording is R. D. Hicks’s translation, first published in 1925. The idea belongs to the Pythagorean tradition, but nothing shows that Pythagoras himself said it.

source.heading: Where the words actually appear

docMeta.dd: Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VIII (Pythagoras), §33
Diogenes Laërtius, reporting Alexander’s excerpts from “the Pythagorean memoirs”
R. D. Hicks (Loeb Classical Library 185; London: Heinemann; New York: Putnam, 1925)

source.excerpt: Right has the force of an oath, and that is why Zeus is called the God of Oaths. Virtue is harmony, and so are health and all good and God himself; this is why they say that all things are constructed according to the laws of harmony. The love of friends is just concord and equality.
trail: Wikiquote’s Pythagoras page lists “Virtue is harmony” under Disputed. It notes that the line “seems to be derived from the account of Diogenes Laertius of Pythagorean doctrines, where he simply describes the statement as a precept of his followers” (Wikiquote ↗).

The exact wording appears in R. D. Hicks’s translation of Diogenes Laërtius 8.33, inside a list of tenets that Alexander “found in the Pythagorean memoirs” (Perseus, Hicks ↗). The Greek reads την τ’ αρετην αρμονιαν ειναι (Perseus, Greek ↗).

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy says that “Pythagoras wrote nothing.” It also says that Diogenes’ account (VIII.24–33) rests on “the Pythagorean Memoirs excerpted by Alexander Polyhistor, which are a forgery dating sometime around 200 BCE” (SEP ↗).
A search of Quote Investigator for “virtue is harmony” returned no article, so Wikiquote is the specialist anchor for this line.
source.excerptNote: The list begins at 8.24 with: “Alexander in his Successions of Philosophers says that he found in the Pythagorean memoirs the following tenets as well.” In Hicks’s note to that passage, the Alexander is Alexander Polyhistor, of the first century BC, and the source is “a Hellenistic document long forgotten.” C. D. Yonge’s older translation gives the same phrase: “virtue is harmony, and health, and universal good, and God.”

author.name: Pythagoras
author.heading: About Pythagoras
author.metaLine: c. 570 – c. 490 BC · Greek philosopher of Samos and Croton
author.bio: Pythagoras was one of the most famous and most argued-over early Greek philosophers. He spent his early years on Samos and later moved to Croton in southern Italy, where most of his philosophical work took place. He wrote nothing, and no one in his own lifetime wrote a detailed account of his thought. In the centuries after him, much later Pythagorean writing was credited to him, which is why so many “Pythagoras quotes” are really school doctrine or later inventions.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Pythagoras
misattribution.intro: Quote sites present “Virtue is harmony” as something Pythagoras said. But the only ancient source for it reports a doctrine of his school, passed on at third hand.

items.why: Pythagoras wrote no books, and no record from his lifetime gives this saying. Diogenes Laërtius gives it as a tenet that Alexander “found in the Pythagorean memoirs” (Lives 8.33, tr. Hicks ↗). Wikiquote files it under Disputed for this reason (Wikiquote ↗).

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls these memoirs, excerpted by Alexander Polyhistor, “a forgery dating sometime around 200 BCE” that assigns “not just Platonic but also Stoic ideas to Pythagoras” (SEP ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: “Virtue is harmony” is a Pythagorean school tenet. It is preserved in Diogenes Laërtius 8.33 from the “Pythagorean memoirs”, and the exact English wording is R. D. Hicks’s 1925 translation (Perseus ↗). It is not a recorded saying of Pythagoras himself.

context.heading: Why harmony mattered to the Pythagoreans
lead: The same passage applies harmony to everything: virtue, health, the good and God are all called harmony, “this is why they say that all things are constructed according to the laws of harmony,” and friendship is “concord and equality.” The idea that order and goodness come from proportion is typical of the Pythagorean tradition. That is why the line sounds like Pythagoras, even though the text it comes from was written in his name long after him.
context.pull: Virtue is harmony, and so are health and all good and God himself.

isPartOf.name: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers

schema.verdictNote: Commonly attributed to Pythagoras, but not his words: a Pythagorean school tenet that Diogenes Laërtius (Lives 8.33) reports from the “Pythagorean memoirs”, which the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls a forgery from around 200 BCE. The true author is unknown; no creator is asserted here.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists 'Virtue is harmony' under Disputed on the Pythagoras page and says it derives from Diogenes Laertius's account of Pythagorean doctrines, a precept of his followers; it gives the Yonge (1853) rendering.

Hicks translation (Harvard University Press, 1972, first published 1925) of DL 8.33 reads 'Virtue is harmony, and so are health and all good and God himself...'; 8.24 introduces the tenets Alexander 'found in the Pythagorean memoirs'; note 19 names Alexander Polyhistor in the first century B.C. and 'a Hellenistic document long forgotten'.
Greek text of DL 8.33 contains 'τήν τ᾽ ἀρετὴν ἁρμονίαν εἶναι καὶ τὴν ὑγίειαν...'.
Yonge translation (Bohn's Classical Library) reads 'virtue is harmony, and health, and universal good, and God'.

SEP: Pythagoras lived ca. 570 to ca. 490 BCE, moved from Samos to Croton, 'wrote nothing'; DL VIII.24–33 is based on the Pythagorean Memoirs excerpted by Alexander Polyhistor, 'a forgery dating sometime around 200 BCE' assigning Platonic and Stoic ideas to Pythagoras.
